sources.title: Peter Hackman, Elementary Number Theory
sources.locator: Chapter E, §E.I “Primes as Sums of Squares” and §E.II “Composite Numbers” in full, printed pp. 143–155 (PDF pp. 154–166), including all numbered results, examples, and exercises through E.II Exercise 7

contents.name: §E.I, Primes as Sums of Squares
E.I.1 Lemma, Thue’s Lemma
E.I.2 Theorem, a prime is a sum of two squares iff it is 2 or 1 modulo 4
E.I.3 Theorem, two different representations of an odd integer give a nontrivial factorisation
E.I.3 prime corollary, uniqueness of the positive odd-even representation
E.I.4 Example, writing 73 as 3 squared plus 8 squared by Extended Euclid
E.I.5 Example, an infinite-descent algorithm for a prime two-square representation
contents.reason: This is a third construction algorithm for the same prime theorem; the pair retains both the finite-collision and Extended-Euclid routes, while the descent recurrence has no distinct downstream claim here.

contents.name: E.I Exercise 1, primes represented by x squared plus 2y squared
contents.reason: Representation by the distinct positive-definite form x squared plus 2y squared belongs with the classification and reduction of integral binary quadratic forms.

contents.name: E.I Exercise 2, primes represented by x squared minus 2y squared
contents.reason: The indefinite norm form x squared minus 2y squared is governed by Pell equations and their norm-one orbits, rather than the positive two-square norm developed here.

contents.name: E.I Exercise 3, primes represented by 2x squared plus 3y squared or x squared plus 6y squared
contents.reason: These congruence criteria concern different positive-definite binary quadratic forms and require the equivalence and reduction machinery assigned to that topic.

contents.name: E.I Exercise 4, a constructive Extended-Euclid proof of Thue’s Lemma
contents.reason: The exercise is an alternative algorithmic proof of the retained Thue statement; its continued-fraction and Euclidean-approximation structure belongs with the dedicated approximation development.

contents.name: E.I Exercise 5, compute large prime representations with Jacobi and Extended Euclid
contents.reason: The large-input computation exercises the approximation algorithm rather than adding a new representation theorem or boundary case to this pair.

contents.name: §E.II, Composite Numbers
E.II.1 displayed two-square product identity
E.II.1 Lemma, a product of represented positive integers is represented
E.II.2 Theorem, the prime-exponent characterisation of sums of two squares
E.II.2 proof subclaim, a 3-modulo-4 prime dividing a two-square sum divides both coordinates
E.II.3(a) Example, the two representations 221 equals 10 squared plus 11 squared and 14 squared plus 5 squared
E.II.3(b) Example, 539 equals 7 squared times 11 and is not a sum of two squares
E.II.3(c) Example, 833 equals 28 squared plus 7 squared
E.II.4 Theorem, Proper Representation
E.II.5 Lemma, coprime primitive represented factors have a primitive product representation
E.II.6 Lemma, powers of a 1-modulo-4 prime have primitive representations
E.II.7(a) Example, 289 equals 15 squared plus 8 squared primitively
E.II.7(b) Example, 34 equals 3 squared plus 5 squared primitively
E.II.7(c) Example, 833 has a nonprimitive representation and no primitive representation
E.II.7(d) Example, 68 equals 8 squared plus 2 squared and has no primitive representation
E.II.8(a) Corollary, a product of primitive represented integers not both even is primitively represented
E.II.8(b) Corollary, every divisor greater than one of a primitively represented integer is primitively represented
E.II Exercise 1, classify 112, 851, 829, 629, and 605 for ordinary and primitive representation
E.II Exercise 2, explicit bijections between representations of odd m and 2m, including primitive representations
E.II Exercise 3, four essential representations of 9061 and the lattice-point count
contents.reason: The exact number of ordered signed representations is the r_2 divisor-sum problem assigned to the later representation-count development.

contents.name: E.II Exercise 4, every nonzero residue modulo a prime is a sum of two squares
E.II Exercise 5, insolubility of y squared equals x cubed plus 7
contents.reason: This isolated Mordell-type Diophantine equation belongs to elliptic and higher Diophantine geometry, whose descent and curve machinery is outside the present elementary track.

contents.name: E.II Exercise 6, criterion for minus one to be a quadratic residue modulo n
E.II Exercise 7, two distinct representations by x squared plus D y squared force compositeness
contents.reason: The parameter-D identity and its equivalence classes concern general positive-definite binary quadratic forms, not only the principal two-square form.

sources.title: William Stein, Elementary Number Theory: Primes, Congruences, and Secrets
sources.locator: §5.7 “Sums of Two Squares” in full, printed pp. 117–121 (PDF pp. 123–127), ending before §5.8 Exercises

contents.name: §5.7, Sums of Two Squares
Theorem 5.7.1, a positive integer is a sum of two squares iff every 3-modulo-4 prime has even exponent
SAGE Example 5.7.2, a naive search for a two-square representation
contents.reason: The brute-force Sage loop is a software demonstration rather than a mathematical result or proof boundary, and the companion already gives hand-verifiable constructions.

contents.name: Definition 5.7.3, Primitive
Lemma 5.7.4, a number divisible by a 3-modulo-4 prime has no primitive representation
Proof of Theorem 5.7.1, necessity from a primitive reduction
Identity (5.7.1), a product of two sums of two squares is a sum of two squares
Lemma 5.7.5, continued-fraction approximation with denominator at most n
contents.reason: This approximation lemma is part of the continued-fraction proof route and belongs with the dedicated Diophantine-approximation development rather than the chosen Thue-pigeonhole route.

contents.name: Proof of Theorem 5.7.1, sufficiency via continued fractions
contents.reason: The proof is a genuinely different continued-fraction route whose prerequisite approximation theorem is assigned to the later continued-fraction page; the present theorem is proved locally by Thue's lemma.

contents.name: Remark 5.7.6, the proof gives an efficient representation algorithm
contents.reason: The efficient algorithm depends on the continued-fraction convergents used in Stein's proof and is an application for the planned approximation companion.

contents.name: SAGE Example 5.7.7, the continued-fraction algorithm for a 10-digit prime
contents.reason: This computation demonstrates the continued-fraction algorithm on a large input and belongs with the page that develops that algorithm and its convergents.
